newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Investors fret over next Israeli finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Investors fret over next Israeli finance chief.

text.p: Foreign investors' praise for the package of economic measures undertaken by Israel this week is shadowed by concerns over who will become finance minister, foreign bankers and analysts said on Thursday.
After a series of intense late-night meetings Monday and Tuesday, the government announced changes in its exchange rate regime and a package of foreign currency liberalisation.
In response, the Bank of Israel cut interest rates a sharp 1.2 percentage points to 12.7 percent.

But Finance Minister Dan Meridor, who had opposed some of the moves, announced his resignation and charged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had used the measures as a lever to force him out of the government. Meridor and Netanyahu have been long-time rivals in the ruling Likud party.
"The medium-sized cloud on the horizon is who replaces Meridor," said Stephen Levey, Israel analyst for Carnegie Emerging Markets in London.
"Foreign investors will be sad to see Meridor go because he represents good sense and sound economic policies," said Roger Hornett of Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.

The two most widely touted candidates to succeed Meridor are National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon and Yaacov Neeman, a former Treasury director-general and, for a brief time, justice minister.
"If a person like Neeman goes to the ministry, no one really knows him," said a foreign investment banker who spoke on condition of anonymity.

"Sharon on the other hand is a well-known figure worldwide and not necessarily always positively. I would imagine that foreign investors hearing that Sharon was foreign minister might be more concerned," the banker said.
Sharon, a controversial former general, has held cabinet posts in various Likud governments, including defence, housing and industry and trade.

Neeman, a lawyer, quit as justice minister in the Netanyahu government after two months, when he was indicted on charges of obstructing justice and lying under oath in a case before he joined the cabinet. He has since been exonerated.
Analysts said they were concerned Sharon would show less budgetary discipline than Meridor.

"Meridor was an excellent finance minister. He did very well with the budget package he put together," said Levey. "I think the 1997 budget is safe and the privatisation process is safe because it is not in the finance minister's hands. But with the 1998 budget under Sharon I would be very concerned."
Other analysts were more sanguine, saying Netanyahu would not appoint a finance minister who threatened to undermine Israel's hard-won fiscal restraint.
"With Sharon there's some negative history," said one overseas banker based in Tel Aviv. "But I think that policy is what counts, not those implementing it."
Analysts discounted the impact of the exchange rate reform, saying it would not lead to any immediate change in the shekel rate.

The reform adjusts the diagonal rate at which the Israeli currency depreciates over the year against a basket of foreign currencies to a minimum of four percent from six percent. The band in which the shekel rate can fluctuate was widened at its upper end but left unchanged at its lower end.
But most analysts said the interest rate cut would be a bonus for Israel's stock market.

"This is an interest rate-driven market rather than an earnings-driven market," said Levey. "Last week people were looking for a 30 basis point cut and now they've got a 120 basis point cut. In addition, people are looking for cuts of 90-100 basis points over the next three to four months."
